PssSol.xml.title: Psalms of Solomon

fields.introduction:
The Psalms of Solomon (PssSol) is a Jewish pseudepigraphical collection of eighteen poetic psalms composed in Judea during the turbulent midpoint of the first century BCE (ca. 63–37 BCE) and brought into its final composite form prior to the fall of Jerusalem in 70 CE. Pseudepigraphically attributed to King Solomon—celebrated in biblical tradition for his wisdom, proverbs, and thousands of songs (cf. 1 Kgs 4:32; canonical Ps 72)—the collection captures the acute communal trauma, factional conflict, and fervent eschatological longings of Jewish society following the collapse of Hasmonean sovereignty and the Roman conquest of Jerusalem by Pompey the Great in 63 BCE.

Although not preserved in the canonical Hebrew Bible or among the Dead Sea Scrolls, the Psalms of Solomon was faithfully transmitted through Christian ecclesiastical channels in the Greek East. Ancient canonical catalogues—most notably the fifth-century table of contents (Pinax) of Codex Alexandrinus (which lists the eighteen psalms among the antilegomena following 1–2 Clement), the sixth-century Synopsis Scripturae Sacrae (pseudo-Athanasius), and the ninth-century Stichometry of Nicephorus (which measures the work at 2,100 stichoi)—demonstrate that the collection was read and copied as a significant ecclesiastical appendix to Septuagint and New Testament codices.

Spanning an array of classical biblical poetic genres, the collection includes communal laments (PssSol 1, 2, 8), individual prayers of thanksgiving and penitence (PssSol 3, 5, 6, 9, 13, 15, 16), wisdom and didactic reflections (PssSol 4, 10, 14), and royal messianic hymns (PssSol 17, 18). It stands alongside the Dead Sea Scrolls as one of the most vital textual witnesses to late Second Temple Palestinian Jewish theology, articulating a profound theodicy in the face of foreign subjugation, an acute ethical dualism between the "righteous" and "sinners," an explicit hope in the bodily resurrection of the righteous to eternal life, and the most detailed pre-Christian portrait of a personal, Davidic Messiah (huios Dauid) in ancient Jewish literature.
fields.provenance:
Date and Historical Setting

The historical backdrop of the Psalms of Solomon is anchored in the dramatic political convulsions of first-century BCE Judea. Three psalms in particular—2, 8, and 17—contain vivid, transparent historical allusions that allow modern scholars to date their composition with remarkable precision:

  • The Siege and Fall of Jerusalem (63 BCE): Psalm 8 recounts the approach of a foreign conqueror from the ends of the earth who was welcomed by the city's corrupt leadership, assaulted the fortified walls with battering rams (8:15–21; cf. 2:1), and desecrated the Temple sanctuary, trampling the holy altar with pagan feet (2:2). As first recognized by F. K. Movers in the nineteenth century, this corresponds exactly to the Roman siege led by Pompey the Great in 63 BCE, intervening in the civil war between the Hasmonean brothers Hyrcanus II and Aristobulus II as recounted by Flavius Josephus (Ant. 14.3–4; J.W. 1.6–7).
  • The Denunciation of Late Hasmonean Usurpation: The psalms deliver a scathing theological polemic against the native Hasmonean priest-kings (Aristobulus II, Hyrcanus II, and Alexander Jannaeus). The psalmist charges them with unlawfully arrogating royal majesty to themselves without Davidic covenantal legitimacy (17:5–8) and defiling the altar, sanctuary, and sacrificial rites with ritual impurity and incest (8:11–13, 22; 2:3–14). The Roman assault is thus interpreted not as a tragic defeat of God's people, but as a deserved divine punishment upon an apostate aristocracy.
  • The Ignominious Fate of Pompey (48 BCE): Psalm 2:26–27 provides a decisive terminus post quem for the collection, describing the dishonorable end of the Roman conqueror: "I did not have to wait long before God showed me the insolent one lying dead on the mountains of Egypt, despised more than the smallest on land and sea, his body decomposed by the waves with no one to bury him." This matches Pompey's assassination on the beach of Pelusium in Egypt in 48 BCE following his defeat at the Battle of Pharsalus, where his headless body was left exposed on the shore.
  • Herod the Great's Siege and the Atkinson Redating Thesis: While earlier scholars (e.g., Ewald, Bretschneider, Cellier) proposed obsolete dates ranging from Ptolemy I to Titus, Kenneth Atkinson ("Toward a Redating of the Psalms of Solomon," 1998; "Herod the Great, Sosius, and the Siege of Jerusalem," 1996) argues that Psalm 17 reflects the bloody siege of Jerusalem in 37/36 BCE by Herod the Great and the Roman general Gaius Sosius. Atkinson suggests that the collection spans the historical transition from the late Hasmonean period to the early Herodian era (ca. 63–30 BCE), reflecting an ongoing community that weathered both crises.

The complete absence of any allusion to the cataclysmic destruction of the Second Temple in 70 CE firmly establishes that the collection attained its final redacted form before 70 CE, with the majority of psalms composed between 63 and 40 BCE (as proposed by R. B. Wright, E. P. Sanders, and M. de Jonge).

Authorship, Provenance, and Sectarian Milieu

The collection was composed in Judea, almost certainly in Jerusalem or its immediate environs. The identity of the community behind the psalms has been one of the most vigorously debated problems in Second Temple scholarship:

  • The Pharisaic Hypothesis: Pioneered by Julius Wellhausen (Die Pharisäer und die Sadducäer, 1874) and popularized by H. E. Ryle and M. R. James in their landmark edition Psalms of the Pharisees, Commonly Called the Psalms of Solomon (1891), this view held that the authors were Pharisees opposing the Sadducean Hasmonean hierarchy. The thesis was supported by the poems' fierce devotion to Torah, belief in divine sovereignty alongside human free will, insistence on bodily resurrection, and strict purity regulations. Mikael Winninge (Sinners and the Righteous, 1995) has defended a modified version of this stance.
  • The Post-Qumran Critique: The discovery of the Dead Sea Scrolls decisively shattered the exclusivity of the Pharisaic identification. As demonstrated by J. O'Dell (1961) and R. B. Wright (1972), doctrines such as divine retribution, bodily resurrection, messianic deliverance, and hatred for Hasmonean corruption were not distinctive to Pharisees, but were widely shared across the broader apocalyptic and pietistic streams of Palestinian Judaism. The internal evidence proves firmly that the authors were non-Sadducean, but does not identify them uniquely as Pharisees.
  • The Essene and Qumran-Adjacent Hypotheses: André Dupont-Sommer (1973) proposed that the psalms originated among the Essenes, a hypothesis further refined by P. N. Franklyn (1987), who posited a previously unrecorded branch of the Essene movement. However, no copies or fragments of the Psalms of Solomon have been found among the Dead Sea Scrolls, and the references to fleeing into the wilderness (PsSol 17:16) reflect temporary flight during siege warfare rather than permanent communal withdrawal to Qumran.
  • The Zadokite Displacement Model: Advanced by Heerak Christian Kim (Zadokite Propaganda in the Late Second Temple Period, 2014), this theory links the collection with displaced Oniad/Zadokite priests who were ousted from the Temple cult by the Hasmoneans and who produced polemical psalms protesting their disenfranchisement and calling for cultic restoration.
  • The Modern Consensus: Unknown Jerusalem Pietists: The dominant contemporary perspective, articulated by Kenneth Atkinson (I Cried to the Lord, 2004) and endorsed by E. P. Sanders, concludes that the authors cannot be identified with any known historical sect (Pharisees, Sadducees, or Essenes). Rather, the psalms were composed by an unknown, pietistic Jerusalem circle—self-designated as "the assemblies of the devout" (συναγωγαὶ ὁσίων, PsSol 17:16)—rooted in traditional Hasidic piety (Büchler 1922; Flusser 1984; Hann 1988) and maintaining strict covenantal fidelity amid socio-political marginalization.

Original Language and Translation Character

The overwhelming majority of modern scholars (including Ryle and James, G. B. Gray, Emil Schürer, Joseph L. Trafton, and Robert B. Wright) maintain that the Psalms of Solomon was originally composed in Hebrew, and subsequently translated into Greek, from which the Syriac version later derived (or, as Trafton and Grant Ward argue, with both versions reflecting independent access to a common Hebrew Vorlage). The case for a lost Hebrew original rests on several converging lines of philological evidence:

  • Pervasive Semitic Syntax: The Greek text exhibits continuous coordinate clauses linked by καί, construct-state periphrases, rigid Hebrew word order, and idioms that represent word-for-word calques of classical biblical Hebrew poetry.
  • Demonstrable Translation Errors: Several obscure or impossible Greek readings are explicable only as misreadings or graphic confusion of Hebrew consonants. For example, at PsSol 2:25, the translator appears to have misread Hebrew rymhl ("to change/alter") as rm'l ("to say"), producing the ungrammatical Greek phrase τοῦ εἰπεῖν. Similarly, at PsSol 2:26, the description of Pompey's insolence (ἡ ὑπερηφανία αὐτοῦ) likely reflects a graphic confusion of Hebrew g'wtw ("his pride") for gwytw ("his corpse").
  • Intertextual Dependence with Baruch: The undeniable literary relationship between Psalm of Solomon 11 and Baruch 5:5–8 demonstrates that one work drew upon the other. Because PsSol 11 displays superior poetic unity and structural cohesion, scholars widely judge that Baruch translated or adapted a pre-existing Hebrew Vorlage of Psalm 11.
  • The Syriac Evidence: Comprehensive philological analysis by Joseph L. Trafton (1985, 1986) indicates that while the Syriac text shows close affinity with the Greek manuscript family of Group 253, several Syriac readings preserve genuine Semitic idioms or variants that suggest access to a Semitic Vorlage.

A vocal minority (beginning with Hilgenfeld in 1871 and revisited by some contemporary linguists) has argued for direct Greek composition in intentional imitation of the Septuagint. However, as Kenneth Atkinson notes in the NETS commentary, the persistent "lexical stereotyping" (e.g., translating Hebrew hasid uniformly as ὅσιος and hesed as ἔλεος) and syntactical stiffness are standard hallmarks of translation Greek rather than Hellenistic Greek composition.
fields.themes:
Divine Justice and Theodicy (Dikaiokrites)

The overarching theological concern of the Psalms of Solomon is theodicy: defending and justifying the righteousness of God in the face of national disaster, foreign military conquest, and the profanation of the Jerusalem sanctuary (Atkinson 2003). The psalmist continually hails God as the "righteous judge" (δικαιοκρίτης, PsSol 2:15, 32; 8:24–26; 9:2). Rejecting any notion that the Roman conquest demonstrated divine weakness or indifference, the collection insists that God's judgments are entirely upright (2:15). Pompey's assault and the subsequent slaughter of Jerusalem's inhabitants were the direct consequence of the rampant sins, sexual depravity, incest, and cultic corruption practiced by the Hasmonean leadership and priesthood (2:3–14; 8:8–13). In the framework of a prophetic-Deuteronomic covenant theology, history is interpreted through the lens of retribution for apostasy and assurance for the faithful (Chai 2015).

Disciplinary Suffering and Divine Paideia

A distinctive theological contribution of the collection is its sophisticated doctrine of disciplinary suffering (paideia). The psalmist makes a radical distinction between the punitive destruction meted out to defiant sinners and the remedial, paternal chastisement experienced by the righteous:

"He will admonish the righteous person as a beloved son, and his discipline is as that of a firstborn." (PsSol 13:8; cf. 7:3; 10:1–3; 13:6–10)

The righteous are not morally sinless; rather, they commit unintentional faults or sins of ignorance, for which they make immediate atonement through fasting, prayer, and self-humiliation (PsSol 3:7–9). God uses hardship not to destroy the righteous, but to cleanse and refine them, preserving them from the irrevocable doom awaiting the ungodly. As explored in recent rhetorical analysis ("Living Faith in Adversity," 2024), this theological paradigm functioned as a crucial mechanism for psychological resilience and group cohesion under foreign military occupation.

Ethical Dualism: The Righteous vs. The Sinners

The poems structure human society into two diametrically opposed ethical and spiritual camps (Winninge 1995; Werline 2015):

  • The Righteous and Devout (δίκαιοι, ὅσιοι): Those who live in steadfast obedience to the Torah, acknowledge their human frailty, accept divine discipline with humility, and gather in "the assemblies of the pious" (συναγωγαὶ ὁσίων, PsSol 17:16). Their righteousness is grounded not in claim of perfection, but in humble submission to God's covenantal discipline.
  • The Sinners (ἁμαρτωλοί) and Hypocrites (ἀνθρωπάρεσκοι): The arrogant political and religious aristocracy who flaunt divine law, oppress the poor, desecrate the sanctuary, and practice duplicity while outwardly feigning piety (PsSol 4:1–8; 8:8–14).

Eschatology and Bodily Resurrection

The Psalms of Solomon offers one of the clearest and most definitive testimonies to individual afterlife and bodily resurrection in late Second Temple Judaism (George W. E. Nickelsburg 1972/2006; Trocino 2021). The collection teaches an asymmetrical eschatological outcome based strictly on ethical conduct:

  • Resurrection to Eternal Life for the Righteous: "They that fear the Lord shall rise to life eternal, and their life shall be in the light of the Lord, and shall come to an end no more" (PsSol 3:12; cf. 13:11; 14:9–10). Physical death is not the end of the devout; God will raise them to partake of eternal blessedness in the divine presence.
  • Irreversible Perdition for the Wicked: In sharp contrast, there is no resurrection or hope of afterlife for the ungodly. Their destiny is permanent destruction, darkness, and oblivion in Sheol/Hades: "The destruction of the sinner is forever... and their inheritance is Sheol, darkness, and destruction" (PsSol 3:11; 15:10). The wicked are blotted out eternally from God's remembrance.

Davidic Messianism (Psalms 17 and 18)

Psalms 17 and 18 constitute the locus classicus of pre-Christian Jewish expectations of a personal Davidic Messiah (Grant Ward 1995; Scott Reynolds 2017; Atkinson 1999). Repudiating the non-Davidic Hasmonean dynasty that had usurped royal status without covenantal warrant, the psalmist petitions God:

"Behold, Lord, and raise up for them their king, the son of David (υἱὸς Δαυίδ), at the time that you know, O God, to reign over Israel your servant! Gird him with strength to shatter unrighteous rulers, to purge Jerusalem from Gentiles who trample her down in destruction..." (PsSol 17:21–22)

The Messiah's person and mission are portrayed with extraordinary theological nuance:

  • A Human, Davidic King: He is not an angelic or transcendent divine figure, but an earthly mortal ruler belonging to the Davidic line, reigning as God's faithful vice-regent over a reconstituted Israel.
  • Pure from Sin: He is uniquely consecrated and "pure from sin" (καθαρὸς ἀπὸ ἁμαρτίας, PsSol 17:36), so that he may govern a holy people in justice and wisdom.
  • Spiritual and Non-Militaristic Conquest: Remarkably, while he destroys the wicked and purges Jerusalem of pagan oppressors, he does not rely on conventional imperial militarism: "He will not place his trust in horse and rider and bow, nor will he multiply gold and silver for war, nor will he gather confidence from a multitude for the day of battle" (PsSol 17:33). Instead, echoing Isaiah 11:1–5 and canonical Psalm 2:9, he strikes the earth with the word of his mouth and rules through the power of the Holy Spirit (PsSol 17:35–37).
  • Universal Ingathering and Worldwide Renown: He gathers the dispersed twelve tribes of Israel, reapportions them upon their ancestral land, and brings Gentile nations under his peaceful, righteous dominion to serve God and behold the glory of the Lord (PsSol 17:26–31).

The Text-Critical Crux at Psalm 17:32: Christos Kyrios

A famous and fiercely debated text-critical crux occurs at Psalm 17:32, where all extant Greek manuscripts unanimously read the nominative phrase: καὶ βασιλεὺς αὐτῶν χριστὸς κύριος ("and their king shall be the Lord Messiah" or "Christ [the] Lord").

Beginning with A. Carrière in 1870, a long line of critical scholars (including Julius Wellhausen, Alfred Rahlfs, G. Buchanan Gray, and K. G. Kuhn) considered this reading impossible for a pre-Christian Jewish text. They argued that kyrios was an early Christian copyist's messianizing scribal corruption (paralleled in the Septuagint of Lam 4:20) and emended the nominative to the genitive χριστὸς κυρίου ("the Lord's anointed", reflecting Hebrew məšîaḥ YHWH), which occurs naturally in PsSol 18:5 and 18:7.

However, Robert R. Hann ("Christos Kyrios in PsSol 17.32: 'The Lord's Anointed' Reconsidered," NTS 31 [1985]: 620–27), supported by Robert B. Wright (2007) and Joseph L. Trafton, has mounted a compelling defense of the transmitted manuscript text. Hann demonstrates that christos kyrios represents a genuine, pre-Christian anarthrous messianic title combining the term "anointed" with the political/royal honorific "lord" (a stylistic convention seen in contemporary Hellenistic and late Second Temple honorific titles). Rather than being an anachronistic Christian interpolation, PsSol 17:32 represents the direct historical and linguistic precedent for the unique angelic announcement in Luke 2:11: "for to you is born this day in the city of David a Savior, who is the Lord Messiah" (σωτὴρ ὅς ἐστιν χριστὸς κύριος).
fields.status:
The Online Critical Pseudepigrapha presents the Greek text of the Psalms of Solomon based on the critical text of Alfred Rahlfs as computerized and prepared by Craig A. Evans, systematically collated and enriched with the manuscript collations of Robert B. Wright (The Psalms of Solomon: Color Images of Greek and Syriac Manuscripts, CD-ROM, 2003; and The Psalms of Solomon: A Critical Edition of the Greek Text, 2007).

In accordance with the OCP digital architecture, the eighteen psalms are structured into individual verse and colometric units with an interactive critical apparatus documenting all textual variants across the eleven primary Greek manuscript witnesses.

The Greek critical text is accompanied by two complete parallel modern translations across all eighteen psalms:

  • English: G. Buchanan Gray's classic scholarly translation (from R. H. Charles, ed., The Apocrypha and Pseudepigrapha of the Old Testament, 1913), with modernized punctuation, colometric layout, and poetic alignment.
  • French: Joseph Viteau and François Martin's critical French translation (Les Psaumes de Salomon: Introduction, texte grec et traduction, 1911).

The Greek Manuscript Tradition

The Greek text of the Psalms of Solomon survives in eleven manuscripts dating from the tenth to the sixteenth century CE. Through the stemmatic analyses of Robert R. Hann (The Manuscript History of the Psalms of Solomon, 1982), Robert B. Wright (The Psalms of Solomon: A Critical Edition of the Greek Text, 2007), and Felix Albrecht (Göttingen Septuagint XII,3, 2018), these witnesses are classified into four distinct textual families, alongside ancient indirect witnesses:

253 V Città del Vaticano, Biblioteca Apostolica Vaticana, Vat. gr. 336 (olim 253) 11th–12th c. Group 253: Primary and most reliable witness to the earliest reconstructible archetype. Closely allied to the Greek Vorlage underlying the ancient Syriac translation.
655 o Città del Vaticano, Biblioteca Apostolica Vaticana, Ottob. gr. 60 16th c. Group 253: Discovered after Rahlfs (1935); direct descendant and close congener of MS 253.
659 p Città del Vaticano, Biblioteca Apostolica Vaticana, Ottob. gr. 384 16th c. Group 253: Discovered after Rahlfs (1935); congener of MS 253 and 655.
260 H (Hauniensis) Copenhagen, Det Kongelige Bibliotek, GkS 6 fol. ("Bible of Niketas") 10th–11th c. Group 260: Oldest surviving complete Greek manuscript; principal representative of the widespread "Bible of Niketas" Byzantine recension.
149 A (Augustanus) Wien, Österreichische Nationalbibliothek, Theol. gr. 11 (olim 149) 11th c. Group 260: Direct congener and copy of MS 260; basis of David Hoeschel's rediscovery and the 1626 editio princeps.
471 M (Mosquensis) Moscow, State Historical Museum, Syn. gr. 147 (olim Athos, Iviron) 12th–14th c. Group 260: Important secondary witness of the Niketas recension, collated by Oscar von Gebhardt.

629 C (Casanatensis) Rome, Biblioteca Casanatense, MS 1908 (olim Casanat. 715) 12th–14th c. Group 629: Preserves a mixed textual tradition exhibiting contamination across Groups 253 and 336.
769 B (Benaki) Athens, Benaki Museum, MS 5 (olim Athos, Great Lavra) 12th–14th c. Group 629: Close congener of MS 629, collated on Mount Athos by Gebhardt.

Ancient Indirect Attestation

  • Codex Alexandrinus (MS A, 5th century CE): Listed in the table of contents (Pinax) under disputed books (antilegomena) immediately following 1–2 Clement with the entry ΨΑΛΜΟΙ ΣΟΛΟΜΩΝΤΟΣ ΙΗ ("Eighteen Psalms of Solomon"). The folios containing the text at the very end of the great codex were lost prior to the modern era, but the entry proves its canonical reception in late antique Egypt.
  • Patristic Stichometries: Cited in the pseudo-Athanasian Synopsis Scripturae Sacrae (early 6th c.) and the Stichometry of Nicephorus (Patriarch of Constantinople, 9th c.), which reckons the work at 2,100 stichoi among the ecclesiastical books.

The Syriac Tradition

The Psalms of Solomon is also preserved in the Syriac tradition across five manuscripts (critical edition by W. Baars, 1972):

  • MS S (7th century CE): A fragmentary marginal text preserved in the margin of a manuscript of the Hymns of Severus of Antioch (British Library, Add. 14538).
  • The Complete Syriac Codices: Manchester, John Rylands Library, Syr. 9 (the celebrated 16th-century "Harris codex"); Birmingham, Selly Oak Colleges, Mingana Syr. 163; Cambridge, University Library, Add. 2012; and Jerusalem, St. Mark's Monastery, Syr. 161.

In the Syriac manuscripts, the eighteen psalms are appended directly to the Odes of Solomon, numbered continuously as Odes 43–60. Philological evaluations by Joseph L. Trafton (1985) demonstrate that the Syriac translation differs from the Greek in only about 62 verses (roughly 10%) and shows an intimate affinity with the Greek archetype of Group 253, while in several passages reflecting independent Semitic idioms.

History of Printed Editions

  • Editio Princeps (1626): First printed by the Jesuit scholar Juan Luis de la Cerda in his Adversaria Sacra (Lyon, 1626), based on a transcript of MS 149 rediscovered in Augsburg by David Hoeschel (1556–1617).
  • Oscar von Gebhardt (1895): Die Psalmen Salomo’s; the foundation of modern stemmatic criticism, expanding the known Greek witnesses from five to eight manuscripts through Mount Athos discoveries.
  • Alfred Rahlfs (1935): Septuaginta; incorporated eight manuscripts, providing the widely adopted standard chapter and verse numbering.
  • Robert B. Wright (2007): The Psalms of Solomon: A Critical Edition of the Greek Text; the first complete edition to collate all eleven Greek manuscripts and four Syriac codices with high-resolution digital imaging.
  • Felix Albrecht (2018): Psalmi Salomonis (Göttingen Septuagint XII,3); the definitive monumental edition providing exhaustive stemmatic apparatus, patristic citations, and orthographic documentation.

4Q548.xml.title: 4Q548 (Dualistic Fragments in Aramaic)

fields.introduction: 4Q548 represents the remnants of an Aramaic text unknown before the Qumran discoveries. The text survives in only three small fragments whose genre is uncertain. Nevertheless, the document is significant because of its clear dualistic themes.
fields.provenance:
The scribal hand of the manuscript 4Q548 has been dated to the second half of the first century BCE (Puech, DJD 31: 393), though the exact date of the composition itself is unknown. Since the fragments of 4Q548 were recovered from Qumran cave four, the document was evidently read by some in that sectarian community. In general, though, the Aramaic texts among the Dead Sea Scrolls are thought to have been penned by Jews outside the movement.

4Q548 may be related to two other Aramaic compositions among the Dead Sea Scrolls, although it does not overlap textually with either. 4Q548 bears some broad similarities (e.g., first-person address and dualism) with Visions of Amram (4Q543–547). However, the resemblance is not close enough to warrant identifying 4Q548 as an additional copy of Visions of Amram. A more likely association is found between 4Q548 and 4Q580, another highly fragmentary Aramaic text with an interest in dualism and a first-person point of view. The physical shape of their largest surviving fragments (4Q548 1–2; 4Q580 2) suggests that they may have been part of the same scroll. It is not clear, though, whether 4Q548 and 4Q580 stem from the same composition or whether they were two independent compositions copied on the same roll.
fields.themes:
The composition, or at least the literary unit that has survived in these fragments, is couched in a first-person address, perhaps indicating a setting of either patriarchal instruction or revelatory discourse.

The surviving text exhibits a strongly dualistic outlook, evident in light/darkness dichotomies. We also find an opposition between “sons of light” and “sons of darkness,” language which is typically associated with so-called Qumran sectarian texts penned in Hebrew. In fact, 4Q548 is the only place this terminology is found in the Aramaic Dead Sea Scrolls.
fields.status:
Transcription

The present edition of 4Q548 was created on the basis of multiple image sets now available on the open-access Leon Levy Dead Sea Scrolls Digital Library developed by the Israeli Antiquities Authority in partnership with Google (http://www.deadseascrolls.org.il/explore-the-archive/manuscript/4Q548-1). For their original transcription, the OCP editors consulted a broad set of images, ranging from scans of the early PAM image plates from 1960 to full spectrum color and infrared digital images taken as recently as 2013.

Since our knowledge of 4Q548 is limited to the three fragments available, we adopted a conservative approach to reconstructions, only supplying the odd character or word at the fringes of fragments when the reading was highly likely due to context. The edition also includes a fresh and complete translation based on the OCP transcription.

Apparatus

The apparatus included in the OCP edition aims to consolidate the various ways the text has been transcribed by contemporary scholars. Once our own transcription was solidified it was compared against eight transcriptions found in print editions (see below). The apparatus lists all instances where these disagreed substantially, excluding minor disagreements in diacritical markings.

Relationship between the Fragments

Fragments 1 and 2 likely originated in the same manuscript column. Yet, since their relation is not certain, the OCP edition presents the text of the fragments independently.

… ellipsis Within square brackets an ellipsis indicates an unreconstructed gap in the text due to damage. An ellipsis outside of square brackets in the translation indicates the presence of either indecipherable ink traces or characters of a partially extant word that cannot be translated.
